Blown out by too much pressure. Repair it with a pipe wrench and a repair kit.
Close to bursting (blows out above %1). Put a router in between and set a limit.
There is no water in the network for it to draw. Fill a barrel on the line, or switch on a pump with a source.
Not enough to water (needs %1). Add a pump, shorten the run, or raise the limit on the router feeding it.
Pressure at this emitter: %1 m of head
Cannot water: the line needs at least %1 m more pressure for it. Add a pump, shorten the run, or move some emitters onto another line.
Mains-fed: flows freely while the town water is on.
Lay a pipe on its tile to connect it to your network.
Water left in the main: %1 L.
Pressure is switched off in this game's sandbox options.
Drawing dirty water from open water.
No well or open water in reach: this pump only adds pressure.
Open water is in reach, but the pump is not running.
A well is in reach, but the pump is not running.
Turning it on would add %1 m.
Cap the pressure this router passes downstream:
Arriving at the valve: %1 m of head
Leaving the valve: %1 m of head
Animated water spray drawn over running sprinklers and open fire hydrants. Purely visual; turn off if you prefer no effects or want to save a little performance.
Looping ambient hum played by working machines, such as the electric purifier while it is powered. Turn off for total silence.
Volume of the mod's machine sounds, from 0 (silent) to 100 (loudest).
Pressure that bursts a drip emitter (tenths)

Above this pressure a drip emitter blows out and stops watering until you repair it, just like a real one. In tenths of a metre of water column: 150 = 15.0, well under a pump's 25.0, so a pump on the same line will burst your emitters unless you put a router in between and set a limit. Set to 0 so emitters never burst.
When auto-refuelling, the generator is topped up to this percentage of its tank (100 = full).
A plumbed generator pulls fuel from the network once its tank drops below this percentage of its capacity. Set to 0 to disable auto-refuelling.

Pressure an open, mains-fed fire hydrant holds its network at, in tenths of a metre of water column. 400 = 40.0, well above the household mains (25.0) and a sprinkler's 20.0, because a hydrant is a high-flow tap on the town main. Opening one runs sprinklers far from any barrel with no pump, right up to the day the water is cut, after which the hydrant still yields its reserve but with no pressure. Lower it to make hydrants less of a free pump.

How much water a fire hydrant still holds in its local main once the town water is cut. 1000 by default. While the water service is on the hydrant is mains-fed and effectively bottomless; this is only what is left afterwards, and it drains as you use it. Set to 0 so hydrants run dry the moment the water stops.

How much a pipe is charged for the water its NEIGHBOURS are drawing. 100 = full realism: thirty sprinklers on one line starve each other, and only the ones nearest the pump run. 0 = the pre-4.x behaviour, where every consumer priced its run as if it were alone on the network, so any number of sprinklers ran off a single pump. Lower it if an existing farm stopped working and you would rather not rebuild it into zones.

Pressure the town supply holds the network at, in tenths of a metre of water column. 250 = 25.0, the low end of what a real municipal main runs. A sprinkler needs 20.0, so at the default the mains runs sprinklers on its own. Lower it if you want pumps to still matter before the shutoff.
Town water intake rate (litres per minute)

How much water the town supply pushes into your network each in-game minute. 60 = 3600 litres an hour, three times a pump, because the mains is the fattest source in the game. Lower it if filling your whole reserve before the shutoff feels too easy.

While the water service is still running, a plumbed sink or shower feeds your pipes instead of just drawing from them: it fills your containers and holds the network at mains pressure, so sprinklers run without a pump until the day the water is cut. Turn this off to keep the old behaviour, where plumbing a fixture switched its town water off and gave nothing back.

Pressure a barrel or collector provides on its own floor, in tenths of a metre of water column, from the weight of its own water. 10 = 1.0, which lets a tap draw from about 20 tiles away on the flat. Raise this if taps in your base sit a long way from their barrels.

How much pressure each pipe tile costs, as a percentage of the default. 100 = default. 200 = pipes lose pressure twice as fast, halving how far water travels. Set to 0 so distance never costs pressure and only height and pumps matter.

How water pressure is worked out. Pressure is measured in metres of water column: height above a tap adds pressure, distance along the pipes spends it, and pumps create it. Realistic uses the full model. Simple counts height only, so distance never costs anything. Off restores the old behaviour, where water simply flows downhill however far it has to travel.
Pressure gained per floor of height (tenths)

Pressure a source gains for each floor it sits above what it feeds, in tenths of a metre of water column. 30 = 3.0 per floor, which matches a real storey height. Higher values make rooftop tanks and water towers stronger.
Pumps can draw from rivers and lakes

When on, a pump placed beside open water draws unlimited dirty water from it, which you can then clean with a purifier. Turn this off to keep water scarce: pumps will still work from wells and from your own barrels.

Pressure a powered pump adds to its part of the network, in tenths of a metre of water column. 250 = 25.0, which matches a domestic pressure set. Pumps chained together add up. A sprinkler needs 20.0, so one pump runs sprinklers about 30 tiles away.

How much water a pump draws from a well or open water each in-game minute. 20 = about 1200 litres an hour, which is on the modest side for a real pump. This is the main brake on infinite river water, so lower it if water feels too easy.

How far below itself a pump can still lift water, in tenths of a metre of water column. 70 = 7.0, about two floors, which is the real limit for a surface pump because atmospheric pressure caps suction. A source further down will not prime, no matter how strong the pump is. Raise this if you want pumps to reach deep basements.

How fast the electric purifier's filter wears out with use, as a percentage of the default rate. 100 = default (a full filter cleans about 5000 units of tainted water before it needs repair). 200 = wears twice as fast, 50 = half as fast. Set to 0 so filters never wear out and never need repairing.

When on, rain falling on an open container left outside taints its whole network, so uncovered collection is a gamble whenever the weather turns. Turn off if you would rather open containers only spoil from sitting still.

When on, taps no longer purify tainted water automatically: tainted water stays tainted until you run it through a purifier tile. On by default as the survival baseline; turn it off to have taps serve clean water like vanilla.
When on, a running sprinkler attracts zombies, which is the price you pay for watering a whole area at once. Turn it off if you would rather irrigate quietly.
Days before sealed water goes bad

How many days a sealed container (a covered tank, the pipe network itself, a lidded amphora) may sit with no movement before its water turns tainted. Sealed water keeps for weeks, so this is the long timer. Set to 0 so sealed water never goes bad.
Days before open water goes bad

How many days an open, rain-catching container (a rain barrel, an uncovered amphora) may sit with no movement before its water turns tainted. Open water spoils in days, so this is the short timer. Set to 0 so open water never goes bad on its own (rain can still taint it).

When on, water left sitting in a container or pipe network turns tainted after a while, and rain contaminates any open water left outside. Drawing from a network, refilling it, or town water flowing through it all count as movement and keep it fresh. Turn off to keep stored water clean forever.

Carries water or fuel. Auto-connects into a network. Plumb sinks, showers and toilets; link barrels, rain collectors and vessels. Built from a metal pipe or a fired clay pipe segment. Dismantling gives the metal pipe back, but clay is spent for good. Needs a Pipe Wrench.

Drip emitter. A pipe that waters the crop on its own tile and passes water on. No pressure needed, only water. Too much pressure bursts it, so keep pumps off its line or cap it with a router. Needs a Pipe Wrench.
A pipe plastered out of sight. Carries fluid like a normal one. Reveal it with 'Show pipe network'. Metal pipe or fired clay; clay is spent for good. Needs a Pipe Wrench and a bucket of mixed cement.
A pipe run up a wall. Links floor pipes on both sides and connects different floors. Metal pipe or fired clay; clay is spent for good. Needs a Pipe Wrench.

A vertical pipe plastered into the wall. Links floors out of sight. Reveal it with 'Show pipe network'. Metal pipe or fired clay; clay is spent for good. Needs a Pipe Wrench and a bucket of mixed cement.

A one-way valve: water flows in through the green band (IN) and out through the red band (OUT), never back, capped at the pressure ceiling you set. Put a vessel on its tile and the two sides exchange only through it: a purifier cleans water in transit, a tank buffers it. Rotate with R to aim the OUT side.

Sprinkler. A pipe that waters the whole 3x3 around it, but needs real pressure, which means a pump. It sprays every tile whether or not it is growing, wastes water, and is loud enough to draw zombies. Needs a Pipe Wrench.
Pressure dial. Sits on a pipe; right-click to read the pressure at that point and whether a sprinkler would run there. Needs a Pipe Wrench.

Electric pump. On a pipe run it raises pressure while powered, and chained pumps add up. Beside a well or open water it also draws water into the network. It sucks up from about two floors below but pushes far higher, so place it low. Needs a Pipe Wrench and welding gear.

Electric purifier tank. Put it on a Fluid Router: tainted water enters from the green (IN) side and leaves purified through the red (OUT) side while it has power. The filter wears with use; right-click to repair it with charcoal and ripped sheets. Needs welding gear and clear space above.
